article_text:
Photos fill the frame at the Epson Pano awards 2026 – in pictures

The Epson Pano awards celebrate panoramic photography from first-time entrants and established professionals alike. This year, the 17th iteration, adds a new aerial category to show off the unique format

This gallery is best viewed on desktop

Beautifully strange: Australian landscapes photographed from the sky – in pictures

The Sleeping Giant

Open photographer of the year | Parinacota volcano, Chile | Daniel Viñé Garcia: ‘The original capture was a 360-degree aerial panorama made from 33 individual exposures … I later refined the framing from the full panorama to concentrate the final composition on the volcanoes, the light and the shapes of the landscape.’ Photograph: Daniel Viñé Garcia /The 17th Epson International Pano awards

Fri 23 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT

Double Arch Over Stokksnes

Amateur photographer of the year Vestrahorn Beach, Iceland | Tomas Sanchez Ruiz: ‘When I pulled back the curtain of our hotel room and saw a green glow in the sky, I knew this could be the night we had been waiting for. The black sand was completely covered in freshly fallen, untouched snow. And there I was, finally taking the photograph I had been waiting for, with a smile on my face.’Photograph: Tomas Sanchez Ruiz/The 17th Epson International Pano awards

The Rugby Players

Epson digital art prize Nyeri, Kenya | Preeti and Prashant Chacko: ‘One morning at Solio game reserve in Kenya we were photographing a group of eight rhinos with a few cattle egrets walking among them ... Something suddenly shifted and five of the rhinos broke into a run. We understood in that instant why a group of rhinos is called a crash. Neither of us has ever played rugby, but from the point of view of the egrets this is how we imagine a forward pack must look, heads down and all that weight already committed.’Photograph: Preeti and Prashant Chacko/The 17th Epson International Pano awards

Journey of Life

Category winner - Aerial Lake Magadi, Kenya | Xuejun Long: ‘As the freshwater evaporated, chemical deposits on the lakebed were exposed, forming lots of interconnected patterns. I was lucky to catch this moment and a flock of flamingos flew in, adding life and bringing a dreamy, magical scene from the sky.’Photograph: Xuejun Long/The 17th Epson International Pano awards

X marks the spot in Shanghai

Highest scoring gigapixel image Shanghai, ChinaPhotograph: Vitaly Golovatyuk/The 17th Epson International Pano awards

Double arch on Milford Sound

Category winner - Nature/Landscape Milford Sound/Piopiotahi, New Zealand | Mikel Iraeta: ‘Milford Sound is a place where it rains on average 300 days a year … It is very difficult to have an entire clear night with no rain, no clouds, no moon and for all of this to coincide at the end of September when it is possible to capture the double arc of the Milky Way. The final image is the result of combining 107 different photographs.’Photograph: Mikel Iraeta/The 17th Epson International Pano awards

Center of the Cosmos

Category winner - Built environment New York, USA | Xuecheng Liu: ‘Times Square is one of the most photographed places in the world, so my challenge was to find a perspective that could make such a familiar place feel unfamiliar again. I stitched together 25 frames to create an ultra-wide aerial panorama, with countless points of light resembling stars surrounding the centre of a galaxy.’Photograph: Xuecheng Liu/The 17th Epson International Pano awards

Between Giants

Highest scoring vertical image Indian Ocean, Mauritius HighestPhotograph: Szabi Nemeth/The 17th Epson International Pano awards

The Emerald Arch Over Lofoten

Southeast Asia open photographer of the year Skagsanden beach, Lofoten, Norway | Wutimet Bunyasirisith: ‘The northern lights flared up and curved perfectly around the mountain. The display was so vastly immense that even my 12mm ultrawide lens couldn’t capture the entire scene in a single frame. My only choice was to shoot a panorama. The conditions that night were brutal, freezing cold, biting winds and I had to wade into the icy seawater to get the shot.’Photograph: Wutimet Bunyasirisith/The 17th Epson International Pano awards

Antarctic Nights

The curator’s award Antarctica | Max Terwindt: ‘We had a special license to fly our drones. As it never becomes dark in the Antarctic summer, the sunset slowly faded into the sunrise, so it went from golden hour to blue hour to golden hour again.’Photograph: Max Terwindt/The 17th Epson International Pano awards

Stairs from Earth to Heaven

Category winner - Built environment Reina Sofía Palace of the Arts, Valencia Spain | Sebastian Cantos Navalon: ‘I used a wide-angle lens and created a composite image from eight shots, aiming for the curved lines of the staircase to guide the eye from the ground towards the sky.’Photograph: Sebastian Cantos Navalon/The 17th Epson International Pano awards

Boreal Wings

Second place - Aerial Lofoten Islands, Norway category Photograph: Francesco Dall’Olmo/The 17th Epson International Pano awards

The Sleeping Giant

Open photographer of the year Parinacota, Chile | Daniel Viñé Garcia: ‘After one last burst of light, the landscape gradually took on magenta tones, wrapping the volcanoes and the high-altitude lakes in a particularly special atmosphere.’Photograph: Daniel Viñé Garcia/The 17th Epson International Pano awards

article_text:
Just when you thought you’d seen everything… A three-hour documentary (in its second weekend of release) has earned almost as much as a new comic-book adaptation at the domestic box office.

Although Warner Bros. and DC’s R-rated “ Clayface ” was comfortably at No. 1 with $24 million from 3,458 North American theaters in its debut, A24’s buzzy Elizabeth Holmes doc “ You Can See Everything ” was surprisingly close after defying box office expectations again. The stranger-than-fiction film collected a spectacular $19.5 million while expanding to 2,655 venues in its sophomore outing.

Related Stories

Agents and Indie Producers Argue Incentives Alone Won't Fix Hollywood's Ills

Ticket sales for “You Can See Everything” are 28% above its launch of $15.6 million from 855 theaters, which marked the best start for a nonmusical documentary in 20 years. So far, the Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim-directed movie has earned a huge $45.1 million domestically to date. After capturing the zeitgeist and selling out screenings across the country, awards sages are predicting it could become the first documentary to ever score a best picture nomination at the Oscars.

Popular on Variety

“Opening ‘You Can See Everything’ in 855 theaters was a really smart move, allowing the film to establish itself and build momentum before going much wider,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. “The fact that we’re seeing a documentary deliver such a significant second-weekend increase is remarkable.”

“Clayface” arrived on the lower end of the studio’s expectations of $25 million to $35 million. The antihero adaptation earned another $19 million overseas from 76 markets for a global tally of $43 million. Along with a positive reception, the film seems well-positioned theatrically because it cost just $44 million to produce. That’s a way smaller budget compared to DC’s other recent tentpoles, including this July’s “Supergirl” and 2025’s “Superman.” Although “Superman” was a decent hit with $618 million against a $225 million budget, “Supergirl” was a setback for the newly relaunched comic book studio after bombing with $126 million against a $170 million budget. Meanwhile, DC has found success on streaming with its “Peacemaker” and “Lanterns” shows for HBO Max. DC wanted to keep costs low on “Clayface” because it’s a body-horror thriller that’s much darker than those family-friendly adventures. Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the titular Batman villain, a rising movie star who volunteers for a highly experimental medical procedure after his face is severely disfigured. Audiences enjoyed the film, which holds an “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls.

“Over the years, there have been a dozen spinoffs of superhero villains and antiheroes, from ‘Joker’ to ‘Venom’ to ‘Kraven the Hunter,'” says David A. Gross, who publishes the box office newsletter FranchiseRe. “This picture was wisely conceived as something different, costing a fraction of what those films cost, and it should be profitable when it finishes all ancillary business.”

“Clayface” opened alongside a smattering of new releases, including Laika’s stop-motion animated “Wildwood,” Black Bear’s offbeat romantic comedy “Wicker” and Sony’s literary adaptation “Klara and the Sun,” starring Jenna Ortega.

“Wildwood” debuted at No. 3 with $11 million from 2,718 venues, launched above projections of $6 million to $8 million. It’s a promising start for original animation, which has been challenged in the years following the pandemic. And “Wildwood” has the benefit of sterling reviews (a rare 100% on Rotten Tomatoes) and audience scores (an “A” grade on CinemaScore exit polls), which should help the film stick around beyond its opening weekend. However, this movie carries a hefty $100 million price tag (stop-motion animation is labor-intensive and takes years to produce) and likely won’t turn a theatrical profit.

“This is a very good opening for a new animated film from outside of the studio development and distribution system,” says Gross. “Audiences love this movie, but it needs a very long run to recoup its costs.”

So far, “Wildwood” has collected just $3 million internationally from 11 markets. The movie hails from Laika Studios, best known for making the 2009 stop-motion fantasy “Coraline.” This is the company’s first release since 2019’s “Missing Link,” which opened to $6 million from 3,413 theaters and ended its run with $26 million globally. “Wildwood” was directed by Laika’s CEO Travis Knight and revolves around a teenage girl who travels with a classmate into an enchanted forest after her brother is abducted.

“Wicker” captured fifth place with $5.75 million from 1,471 locations, a strong start for the low-budget film. Black Bear acquired the well-reviewed movie after Sundance for $2.5 million. Olivia Colman stars as an ostracized woman who commissions a local basketmaker to weave her a husband. Her unexpected romance with the creation (Alexander Skarsgård) sparks jealousy in the village.

“Klara and the Sun” collapsed at No. 15 with $720,000 from 880 locations. Sony scaled back the theatrical footprint after reviews panned the movie as “ calamitous ” and “ confoundingly awful .” Luckily, the Taika Waititi-directed adaptation had a modest $20 million budget, so the studio’s inevitable box office losses won’t be too painful. Based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 novel, “Klara and the Sun” takes place in the dystopian future as an obsolete companion android (Ortega) tries to bond with her new owner, a young sick girl named Josie.

Paramount’s video game reboot “Street Fighter” landed in fourth place with $8.6 million from 3,575 theaters in its second weekend, a painful 72% drop from its debut. The movie has generated $46.9 million in North America and $79.6 million worldwide to date. Legendary and video game developer Capcom co-financed “Street Fighter” for $82 million, with Paramount only on the hook for distribution.

Disney and 20th Century’s “Whalefall,” too, took a tumble in its sophomore outing with $3.2 million from 3,065 theaters. The survival thriller, starring Austin Abrams as a scuba diver swallowed by a sperm whale, dropped to 10th place on weekend charts and has earned $14.1 million domestically and $31.1 million globally to date. “Whalefall” cost $60 million and requires substantial staying power, since theater owners keep about half of ticket sales.

Elsewhere, Netflix’s generation-spanning drama “La Bola Negra” earned $245,000 from nine locations — a decline of 12% despite expanding its theater count. So far, the streamer’s awards hopeful has collected $650,000 from two weekends in limited release. Netflix plans to keep “La Bola Negra” in theaters for 45 days, a traditional window in post-pandemic times, before the film’s Netflix release on Dec. 2.

EXCLUSIVE: Amazon MGM Studios is developing a film adaptation of the K.L. Walther novel The Summer of Broken Rules from Sophia Stallone’s newly launched Common Era Projects and Sylvester Stallone ‘s Balboa Productions.

Lauren Hynek and Elizabeth Martin, a screenwriting team with credits like Disney’s 2020 take on Mulan and Netflix’s animated feature Spellbound , will adapt the script. Sophia Stallone will produce for Common Era, alongside Sylvester Stallone and D. Matt Geller for Balboa.

A #1 New York Times and USA Today bestseller published in 2021, Walther’s novel is a YA romance centered on Meredith Fox, who lost her sister, Claire, 18 months ago and shut everyone out. But this summer, she’s determined to join the world again.

Related Stories

Prime Video Germany Names Former Netflix Film Exec Sasha Bühler As Originals Chief

Amazon MGM Studios Japan To Double Investment In Original Content; 'One Piece' & 'Kingdom' Producers Talk IP Strategies - TIFFCOM

The annual family vacation to Martha’s Vineyard seems like the perfect place to reconnect. Her entire extended family is gathering for a big summer wedding, and although Meredith is dateless after being unexpectedly dumped, she’s excited to participate in the traditional Fox family game of assassin that will take place during the week of wedding festivities. Claire always loved the game, and Meredith is determined to honor her legacy. But when Meredith forms an assassin alliance with a cute groomsman, she finds herself getting distracted. Meredith tries to focus on the game and win it for her sister, but she can’t help falling for him. And as the week progresses, she realizes she’s not only at risk of losing the game, but also her heart.

Watch on Deadline

Sourcebooks Fire published the book in May 2021. So far, it’s sold into 19 territories.

Author Walther told us, “It felt like kismet when Sophia and I connected; within ten seconds of speaking with her, it was clear she truly understands the heart of Meredith’s story and I’m beyond excited and thrilled to see how the team brings it to life!”

Most recently, Sophia Stallone announced development on the MGM Television series Bourbon & Lies , based on the bestselling books by Victoria Wilder. She’s producing that project via Callisto Media alongside Balboa, which re-upped its first-look film & TV deal with Amazon MGM at top of year.

Hailing from Pennsylvania, Walther is also known for titles like While We’re Young and We’re a Bad Idea, Right? .

Balboa Productions, Sophia Stallone and Hynek & Martin are represented by Independent Artist Group, Kleinberg Lange Cuddy & Carlo, and Mike De Trana of Anvil Entertainment. Walther is repped by IAG and Eva Scalzo at Speilburg Literary Agency.

article_text:
Kann man Zukunft designen? Und wie lässt sich Demokratie gestalten? Dara Sepehri kam übers Theater in die Kreativwirtschaft und inszeniert heute Räume für seine Kunden. Im "Fantasiemuskel"-Podcast spricht er über Form und Verantwortung

Welche gesellschaftkliche Funktion hat Design? Lassen sich demokratische Prozesse strategisch gestalten? Der Designer Dara Sepehri stellt als Kurator der Designkonferenz "Form / Future" genau diese Fragen. Er blickt dabei nicht vor dem Hintergrund einer klassischen Designausbildung auf sein Feld, denn er fand seinen Weg in die Kreativwirtschaft über die Bühne. Als Regieassistent erlebte er bei Robert Wilson die Vollendung des Reflexionstheaters, entwickelte jedoch mit der Zeit eine, wie er sagt, "gewisse Genervtheit" gegenüber dem Betrieb, die ihn schließlich in die Agenturwelt führte.

Seitdem inszeniert er Räume für Unternehmen; sein Portfolio umfasst Messestände genauso wie die Inneneinrichtung von Geschäften. Dabei geht es dem Vorstandsmitglied des Deutschen Design Club (DDC) darum, Räume zu schaffen, in denen man sich selbst finden kann.

Die Kernkompetenz von Gestalterinnen und Gestaltern liegt für ihn in der Fähigkeit, unterschiedlichste Expertisen zusammenzuführen – und genau das versucht er auch mit "Form / Future". Im Angesicht aktueller Krisen und eines enormen Transformationsdrucks wird Design zur Plattform, um Akteure aus Kreativwirtschaft, Industrie, Politik und Zivilgesellschaft in den Austausch zu bringen. Um den gesellschaftlichen Wandel sinnlich greifbar zu machen, findet die Konferenz an Orten statt, die sich im Übergang befinden. Vergangenes Jahr gastierte sie im Berliner ICC, dieses Jahr landet sie im ehemaligen Flughafen Tempelhof.

Wo fühlt man sich in der Demokratie wohl?

Der Ansatz, Gestaltung als Synthese des Wissens von unterschiedlichen Disziplinen zu verstehen, lässt sich auch auf demokratische Systeme übertragen. Auch sie sind Räume, in denen wir uns wohlfühlen sollten – gleichzeitig wissen wir, dass derzeit viele Menschen die Vorzüge der Demokratie nicht mehr wahrnehmen. Aus einer gestalterischen Perspektive müsse man sich fragen, wo Bürgerinnen und Bürger den demokratischen Staat eigentlich noch positiv erleben.

Wenn man politische Teilhabe als citizen experience begreift, müssen sämtliche physischen und digitalen Kontaktpunkte überprüft werden. Wichtig ist, die Kompetenzen von Design dabei frühzeitig einzubinden, weshalb mehrere Städte Chief Design Officers einsetzen, um strukturelle Entscheidungen in der Verwaltung zu begleiten.

Dass diese Wirkungsmacht von Design oft unsichtbar bleibt, erklärt Sepehri den Monopol-Podcastern Friedrich von Borries und Torsten Fremer an einem plakativen Beispiel: Der Verkaufserfolg eines Autos wird der Autoindustrie zugerechnet, obwohl die Gestaltung häufig einen wesentlichen Anteil daran hat. Und unter Gestaltung versteht er dabei nicht nur das ästhetische Endprodukt, sondern auch die vorangehende Analyse, die sich aus den verschiedensten Feldern speist.

Designerinnen und Designer, so Sepheri, brauchen deshalb nicht nur Fantasie, sondern auch einen starken "Analysemuskel". Wer Räume schaffen will, in denen Menschen sich selbst finden, müsse sie zunächst verstehen. Erst aus dieser Analyse entsteht die eigentliche Kreativität – die dann vielleicht dazu beiträgt, Demokratie weiterzuentwickeln.

article_text:
“All of a Sudden,” “Clarissa,” “La Gradiva,” “The Invite” and “Tender Loving Care” lead the nominations for the 36th edition of The Gothams with four nods each.

The Gotham Film & Media Institute announced nominations for the 36th edition of The Gothams, singling out 42 feature films and 25 performances in 11 award categories. “Clarissa” and “The Invite” were also nominated for best feature, alongside “Club Kid,” “The Debut,” “Dreams in Nightmares,” “Josephine,” “Mouse,” “Paper Tiger,” “Primetime,” “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” and “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.”

Related Stories

Cynthia Erivo's 'Bad Fairies' Adds Kylie Minogue, Jonathan Groff and Catherine Tate to Voice Cast

James Austin Johnson's Trump Stops by 'SNL U.K.' for Meeting With Burnham and Zelenskyy: 'You Don't Have One Guy Who Can Play Trump?'

“It’s a pleasure to announce this year’s nominees. It has been a remarkable year for film, with audiences turning out in theaters for bold, distinctive work from first-time filmmakers and established artists alike,” said Jeffrey Sharp, executive director of The Gotham Film & Media Institute, announcing the nods. “This year’s nominations, alongside our Tributes and the return of the Audience Award, reflect that abundance and celebrate the creative community that has been at the heart of The Gothams for more than three decades.”

“Paper Tiger” James Gray, director; Andrea Bucko, Leonardo Maria del Vecchio, Gary Farkas, James Gray, Anthony Katagas, Andrea Leone, Raffaella Leone, Marco Perego, Carlo Salem, Rodrigo Teixeira, producers (NEON)

The artist seems to be batting at floating signifiers of luxury and taste with a blindfold on

This past summer, content creators began describing their every movement as ‘kinda chic’. It was kinda chic to read a book, kinda chic to birth a child, kinda chic to order coffee without milk. These posts so diluted the meaning of chicness that the word became impossible to define and only possible to desire. With his solo exhibition of readymades, paintings and mixed-media works at Ulrik gallery, Tam Ochiai seems to be batting at floating signifiers of luxury and taste with a blindfold on, working out his feelings towards the fetishisation of consumer goods.

The Yokohama-born, New York-based artist’s 1994 painting Evin is the most direct satirisation of a chic figure. A whimsical feline loiters at a bistro table underneath pointillist Swiss Alps, aka the blue and white peaks and flat red sky of an Evian water bottle (the letters ‘e v i n’ hang in the middle ground – a chic androgynous name, in fact). To her left, cheerful text announcing three films every cinephile needs to know ( Last Year at Marienbad, Jules and Jim and Shoot the Piano Player ), and hovering around her lithe frame, in faint pencil, are diagrammatic lines and annotations. She’s reading? Cahiers du Cinéma. She’s wearing? Yohji Yamamoto. She smells like? ESCAPE by Calvin Klein.

For decades, the artist has been making distinctively wispy paintings like Simone: can you cat my hair?: blue cafe (2000) and Vibrissae (2006), both included here, all sharp, pointed chins and overlarge kawaii eyes, prioritising ornament and affect-laden detail over a rendering of specifics: we’re not sure where the girls are going, only that they’re looking good. The works in this show, most of which were made during the mid-1990s and early 2000s, have started to age, their whites now closer to beige. But unlike what gets labelled ‘vintage’ online, this patina is not merely an aesthetic or pose. In the gallery, Ochiai has also arranged a delightfully high-low collection of ashtrays on slabs of painted wood, readymades meant to taunt the nicotine-addicted. From antique bronze to plastic New York State Lottery merch, the ashtrays bear the smudgy remnants of their actual use.

The show’s title refers to the reflective layer of tissue behind the retinas of some animals, including cats, that enhances their vision in the dark. Another way of seeing, inspired by a new context (the nighttime), using the lightbouncing mechanics of a mirror. The original contexts for Ochiai’s preoccupations – the film festival and the afters; the luxury department store where one might purchase an outfit to wear to such events – tend to be more flatteringly low-lit than the white cube. His series of brand-name shopping bags made rectangular and coated in plastic, sometimes decorated with thumbprints of complementary dabs of paint, offers another opportunity to consider the arbitrary nature of the iconography we have deemed valuable in the free market. Their existence is inescapable, and Ochiai’s intervention mostly serves to remind us of that fact. Though, amid the logos for brands like Gap and United Colors of Benetton, Ochiai has slipped a few curveballs. Greenberg (1992) is not an appropriated bag but a sparse and restrained textual acrylic painting winking at the critics. MoMA (1994)’s frenetic diagram of kapital and other German words in loopy cursive won’t tell us if it’s a reference to Marx or an ad for Kapital, the Japanese denim brand (it is actually from Joseph Beuys’s 1971 pamphlet ‘How the Dictatorship of the Parties Can Be Overcome’, which the Museum of Modern Art once printed on plastic bags and sold as multiples). The chicest of postures requires the scaffolding of intellect, a sense of awareness behind the je ne sais quoi . Ochiai is true to this, not new to this. Influencers beware.

Tam Ochiai: Tapetum Lucidum at Ulrik, New York, 12 September – 24 October

"你是如何组建这个出色的演职团队的？你有两位非常著名的合作者，一个是联合剪辑莱斯·布兰克（Les Blank），另一个是负责内景拍摄的苏布拉塔·米特拉（Subrata Mitra）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "嗯，莱斯·布兰克去过南加州大学，所以我从学校时就认识他。至于苏布拉塔，因为我是萨蒂亚吉特·雷伊电影的超级崇拜者——我喜欢那种视觉风格。我问了一些朋友，他们把我[和他]联系在了一起。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "事实上，我没有能力去挑选[群演角色]，因为我当时太籍籍无名了。当我成功预定了一家电影制片厂[国泰机构]时——这也不容易，因为没有人愿意把场地租给一个对电影一无所知的人——其中一部分条件是：“你租了摄影棚，就要用我们现成的演员。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但这就好像[做]一个画家。你想象你要用#213号红，结果你拿到了#200号红。这是一次全新的探索。这是另一个挑战，另一个创作冲动。我一点也不介意。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你对当时香港的电影界有什么记忆？这是在香港新浪潮真正爆发之前。", "translated": true}, {"type": "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从身体状况来说，我已经不适合拍电影了，但我一直在脑子里拍电影 [指着头部]。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你脑子里现在的这部电影讲的是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我已经在我脑子里把它写好了。但我只是在想，谁能导演它呢？[笑] 谁能导演它呢？", "translated": true}]

article_text:
One of the highlights of this year’s Cannes Classics program—frankly, of this year’s Cannes—was T’ang Shushuen’s 1968 historical drama The Arch , newly restored by the Hong Kong museum M+ and presented in person by the 87-year-old filmmaker herself. This week and next, it plays in the New York Film Festival’s Revivals section, where American audiences will have the chance to see this remarkable work on the big screen.

Based on a Ming Dynasty–set short story by the Chinese American writer Lin Yutang, the film centers on Madam Tung (Lisa Lu), a middle-aged widow and schoolteacher awaiting the delivery of a letter certifying the construction of a ceremonial arch in tribute to her exceptional character and community service—a traditional honor bestowed by the emperor himself. In T’ang’s telling, Madam Tung lives with her teenage daughter, Wei-Ling (Hilda Chou Hsuan), as well as her aging mother-in-law (Wen Hsiu). When their home and schoolhouse is garrisoned by a soldier whose chemistry with both mother and daughter complicates household dynamics, a fateful gesture of selflessness by Madam Tung causes her inner life to unravel.

The film originally premiered at the San Francisco International Film Festival, and, according to T’ang and the team behind the restoration, it was subsequently part of the very first Director’s Fortnight at Cannes in 1969—though that information remains missing from the festival’s website. T’ang’s debut feature, The Arch was made in Hong Kong after she graduated from the University of Southern California; she went on to make three more features in Hong Kong before a career shift to the culinary business led her back to L.A., where she still runs the restaurant Joss Cuisine on Santa Monica Blvd.

What was the atmosphere like at USC when you were a student there in the ’60s?

It was very rudimentary. Almost like a little hut, you know? The classes were attended by very few people—there were freshmen and Ph.D. [candidates] all together, seeing the same film. It was a very free atmosphere. After that, I went to the Columbia Film Industry Workshop at the Columbia [Pictures] studio. You got the atmosphere of really making films [there]. You had to be a Hollywood person, a union person. I was a union person because I wrote a little television script that they liked, and they had to get me into the Writers Guild.

When did you conceive of The Arch , and how did that project begin to come to life?

Probably a couple years after school. I liked literature before going to film school. But I think with film it’s easier to reach an audience than [with] language, writing. And then to study Chinese literature in America doesn’t make sense [ laughs ], and to write in English is not that easy for a foreigner, you know? But film is an international medium. It is visual.

In fact, I showed the script to my professor at USC and he said to me, “Oh, no, you cannot do this. It’s not a film script, because everybody’s feeling is internal.” But I don’t know why he said that. To me, that is why you use the medium of film, because of what you cannot do with another medium.

How did you assemble this amazing cast and crew? You have two really notable collaborators in Les Blank, who co-edited the film, and Subrata Mitra, who shot the interiors.

Well, Les Blank went to USC, so I knew him from school. And Subrata, because I am a great admirer of Satyajit Ray’s films—I loved the visual style. I asked some friends, who connected me [to him].

The Arch has a beautiful and unexpected narrative arc. It starts off as a film about a soldier garrisoned with Madam Tung, her mother-in-law, and her daughter. By the end you discover it’s really about Madam Tung’s deep solitude and compulsion for self-sacrifice. Where did the story come from?

It’s based on a short story by a very famous writer [Lin Yutang]. But all the details are my addition. The [original] story is more about a widow receiving the honor of an arch. I don’t think the story has a daughter or a mother-in-law.

How did you assemble the cast? Among others, you had Roy Chiao Hung playing the captain, who would later become well-known for his work in King Hu’s movies.

Actually, I had no ability to cast [the ensemble characters], because I was so unknown. When I succeeded in booking a film studio [Cathay Organization]—which wasn’t easy either, as nobody wanted to rent to somebody who didn’t know a thing about film—part of the terms were, “You rent the studio, you use our available actors.”

But it’s like [being] a painter. You imagine you’re going to use #213 Red and you get #200 Red. That is a new exploration. It is another challenge, another creative impulse. I didn’t mind that at all.

What do you remember about the film landscape in Hong Kong at the time? This was before the Hong Kong New Wave really broke out.

I am a very simple-minded person. I wasn’t thinking about all that. [It was more like], “Oh, I have this project I want to do,” and I go, without researching the industry. And then I pick up the phone, I call [the studios], you know: “Ah, I want to make this film. Can I?” And they just thought I was crazy, you know? This stupid girl who didn’t know anything.

But I had a friend [named Jeanette Lin Tsui], who was the classmate of my sister. She became a very famous movie star in Hong Kong and married a powerful young director whose name was [Jimmy Wang Yu]. Everybody called him “Kid” . . . I gave them my script, and they submitted it to everybody who would listen to them. So then [people said], “Oh, maybe she’s for real.”

In order to express the internal states of the characters, particularly that of Madam Tung, you use some extraordinary and rather experimental techniques. Were you exposed to the burgeoning avant-garde scene in the Bay Area during your time in California?

Well, I was exposed to film media. That’s exactly what film media is capable of doing, and what any other media [is not]. And at the time, in America, it’s the Flower Generation; in China, it’s the Cultural Revolution. So it was very open. You experiment. My film happened to be born at that time, and I was influenced by that.

What was the reception like when the film premiered at the San Francisco International Film Festival?

Well, the Mayor of San Francisco announced that The Arch and the Beatles film Yellow Submarine (1968) saved the festival. So it was not a bad reception.

Can you talk a little bit about the films you made afterward?

China Behind (1974) is my second film, [made a few] years later. It’s about the Cultural Revolution and has a very documentary style. I used a newsreel cameraman [Chang Chao-tang] to shoot that film.

Of course, China wouldn’t let me shoot it. So I went to Taiwan. I am sorry to say I had to lie; I told them it was an anti-communist film [ laughs ]. In Taiwan, I called the film Freedom Swimmers . So they gave me a lot of assistance—if I needed soldiers, they provided them.

[The next two films] were made because, you know how I was talking to you about the movie star and the husband? They asked me to do a film for them. And I [felt] obligated because they helped me. So, not [films] I wanted to make.

And how did you then become a restaurateur?

Because my mother was ill. I had to stay in Los Angeles. So my siblings said, “Well, why don’t you open a restaurant, so you don’t have to sit by her bedside every minute?” And, you know, it’s easy for a filmmaker to do anything [ laughs ]. So I opened a restaurant.

Are there any films you’d still like to make?

Physically, I’m in no condition to make a film, but I’m constantly making films up here [ points to head ].

What’s the film in your head right now?

It’s about Li Qingzhao, a very famous poetess in the Song dynasty. She experienced the turn of the dynasty, that period. Her life could be as commercial as Gone With the Wind (1939), if you make it like that. [Just] as Scarlett O’Hara was a very talented young Southern lady, [Li] was a very delicate young Chinese lady, and extremely talented. And her love story… Then suddenly her life changed, because the political situation changed. And like, suddenly you see a very strong woman, you know?

I’ve already written it in my head. But I was just asking, who can direct it? [ laughs ] Who can direct it?

Scientists Contest Dating of Van Gogh’s "The Starry Night"

The researchers identified discrepancies between the celestial alignments in June 1889 and Vincent van Gogh’s painted night sky.

Scholars have long accepted June 1889 as the month when Vincent van Gogh painted the iconic blue eddied-sky and idyllic hillside village of "The Starry Night." Yet a new Scientific Reports study published Thursday, October 22, calls for reconsidering that date, suggesting the Post-Impressionist painter may have drawn inspiration from a night sky that appeared a month later.

South Korean researchers Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, Suna Kang, Jungwoo Song, and Ho Jin argue that several celestial forms in the painting contradict the original June 1889 date and are better supported by the conditions of July that same year. The study incorporates tools that analyze star patterns and positions, contemporary weather models, van Gogh's letters, and other methods of inquiry in what the researchers call a "multidisciplinary framework."

"Earlier astronomical readings, constrained by the conventional June dating, reached mutually exclusive conclusions, and the painting’s celestial arrangement was never quantitatively tested," the report's abstract reads. "These findings suggest that the night sky in The Starry Night originated from observation of a specific celestial arrangement, and call for reconsidering the June dating."

In June 1889, the artist was weeks into his harrowing yearlong confinement at a French asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, a few months after he'd famously severed his left ear during a row with painter Paul Gauguin. The view from his asylum window was thought to have inspired his expressionist masterpiece, which is in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in Manhattan.

Issue

The Illusions of the Center-Periphery

kiswah on display at the Islamic Arts Biennale, Jeddah, 2025. Photo by Marco Cappelletti. Courtesy the Diriyah Biennale Foundation.

At the beginning of their journey through the 2025 Islamic Arts Biennale in Jeddah, visitors came across the kiswah of the Holy Kaʽbah, its black silk panels rising almost to the full height of the gallery space, gold embroidery catching the light. It is an object that, for centuries, has been encountered in Makkah, at the center of a particular relationship to place, ritual and devotion. Here, it was encountered differently, retaining its sacred significance within a milieu of other ways of seeing and making.

A few meters away, Abdelkader Benchamma’s Between Each Sky (2025) unfolded across the walls, its ink and charcoal forms animated by projections and organized around seven columns from Makkah. Nearby, Arcangelo Sassolino’s enormous steel disk, Memory of Becoming , turned slowly and almost imperceptibly, coated in industrial oil that shifted with its movement and gravity. As one work invoked geological strata and celestial expanses, the other made visible mass, instability, and transformation. The kiswah —situated in a dedicated hall between these installations—served not as a mere relic explaining or being explained by contemporary works, but as another singular presence within the conversation.

The scene captured something essential about the second edition of the Islamic Arts Biennale, which borrows its title from a recurring phrase in the Qur’an that references the heavens, Earth, “And All That Is In Between.” Its implication is expansive: rather than creating a binary between heaven and Earth, past and present, divine and worldly, it charts the vast field of creation that exists between such categories. The biennale drew on this proposition to explore how faith is experienced through feeling, thinking, and making. It is tempting to read such an exhibition in Saudi Arabia through the tired language of geopolitics: power shifting toward a more distributed, multipolar order, and the art world simply being downstream of everything else. New biennales in new cities, from this perspective, are the cultural correlates of new capitals in a G20 memo. Though it makes for a tidy story, it is neither a complete nor interesting one.

ABDELKADER BENCHAMMA ’s

Between Each Sky , 2024, at the Islamic Arts Biennale, Jeddah, 2025. Photo by Marco Cappelletti. Courtesy of the Diriyah Biennale Foundation.

The more consequential change is not simply the relocation of art-world power to different coordinates on the same map, but the emergence of institutional models that were never trying to be peripheral versions of an existing template in the first place—models built out of distinct histories, distinct relationships between object and audience, distinct ideas of what and for whom an exhibition exists, and distinct ways of understanding how culture accumulates and is transmitted. This emergence runs parallel to a broader global reconfiguration already underway, whereby rising middle powers are exercising greater agency and forging corridors of exchange between the Gulf, Asia, and Africa. Cultural institutions are among the clearest expressions of this development, operating on terms they set themselves. These new centers, in other words, can introduce novel institutional logics: alternative modes of deciding what belongs in an exhibition, what constitutes a cultural encounter, and how relationships between places are built.

article_text:
W hen I see a film a second time during its theatrical run, it’s typically to take someone else who hasn’t yet seen it, at least in part hoping to witness their reaction to a piece of art that excited or moved me in some way. Seeing Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder’s You Can See Everything a second time in New York City on a Saturday night was that impulse writ larger. This is a movie garnering a surprisingly sizable audience, and outsized audience reactions to go along with it; rewatching it in a full 300-seat auditorium offered the opportunity to re-experience that sense of discovery. Perhaps more to the point, almost everyone I knew had seen it already; all I could do was observe strangers.

This documentary, peering into (and helping to create) a hall of mirrors around the famed med-tech scammer Elizabeth Holmes, has become the box office story of the fall, actually rising 25% on its second weekend to gross another $19.5m – a rare feat even given its expanded screen count. With over $45m in North America, it’s already one of A24’s biggest movies ever; it could wind up in the company’s top three, and way up on the list of the highest-grossing nonfiction features. If You Can See Everything isn’t quite an Obsession -level cash cow, it’s probably even more surprising that a three-hour documentary whose existence was only announced about eight weeks ago is on track to make more money than high-profile new releases like Practical Magic 2, Verity and Street Fighter, among others. It’s also outgrossed co-director Oppenheim’s fellow A24 surprise hit Primetime , which has the benefit of genuine movie star Robert Pattinson.

A few of the viewers I spoke with following the 8pm showing of You Can See Everything at New York’s AMC Empire (typically one of the highest-grossing venues in the country for any number of new releases, where Everything is currently showing on three to five screens depending on the time of day) had also seen Primetime, aware of the connection between the two films. Just as many, however, were not high-frequency moviegoers, at least not by New York standards. Despite an obviously youthful demographic – perhaps owing to the high tolerance for hustle and/or bustle required to trek out to Times Square, I couldn’t find anyone over 30 – there were several viewers who hadn’t been to the movies in months. (The answer to the question of what movie they last saw in theaters ranged from the month-old Primetime to the obligatory summer mega-blockbuster The Odyssey to, yes, Obsession.) Hardly anyone claimed to be a documentary aficionado, either; no one cited a recent documentary they had seen in theaters, saying they were more likely to catch that sort of thing on streaming, if at all.

So what drew them to a big-screen experience featuring both an entertainer (Nathan Fielder) and a subject (Elizabeth Holmes) more closely associated with television? Most of the twentysomethings I spoke with had some combination of familiarity with Fielder’s more overtly comic work – one woman said this seemed “on brand” for him – and awareness of the notoriety of Holmes, the latter usually stemming from the non-documentary TV series The Dropout, which also figures into the film. Each seemed to provide a surprise hook for a big-screen feature – like a more thoughtful version of seeing a movie because it has Anne Hathaway or Spider-Man (not that there’s anything wrong with following either of those into the dark). To a cinema diehard, this seemed almost counterintuitive; were people really being enticed into theaters by faces they knew largely from couch-bound TV binges? Was this effectively serving as a three-hour crossover between The Dropout and The Rehearsal?

There was a sense that this unexpected team-up was part of the sell, with the WTF nature of that idea intact. The extra promise, though, seemed to be that You Can See Everything would offer something more surprising and less easily spoiled than a typical streaming event. The 23-year-old sitting next to me said that she got the impression from social media – specifically, clips on Instagram and TikTok – that this was “a cultural moment”, as she put it. Multiple viewers echoed that sentiment about seeing a handful of clips via social media, and hearing buzz indicating that the movie simply was “unlike anything else out [at the movies]” and had to be seen firsthand to be believed - or at least to be experienced with the proper amount of spoiler-free, audience-vibing surprise. Remarkably, though the movie had been out for over a week and already discoursed at least halfway to death online, none of these twentysomething viewers reported having any idea about the unexpected pivot the movie made at its halfway mark – especially impressive given that it involves another marquee name added to the mix.

During the movie itself, that mystery guest felt like she was winning fans in real time; she even got a round of spontaneous applause by describing Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans , as “batshit crazy”. But while early screenings had been described as meeting with rapturous audience engagement driven by the film’s surprises, this one felt more unpredictable in its alternating waves of laughter and murmuring discomfort. Early in the film, Holmes gets teary talking about the potential separation from her children as she prepares to leave for her prison sentence in a few weeks. Both times I’ve watched it with a full audience, Fielder’s reaction – “that must be hard” – drew one of the movie’s biggest laughs, seemingly for how flatly obligatory it sounds. Yet if this moment primed the audience for peals of cringe-comedy laughter or outright derision toward either Fielder’s affect or Holmes’s refusal to accept responsibility for her deception, that’s not exactly how the movie played out. The movie often cuts to Fielder lurking within proximity of the Holmes family during tense moments; though the mechanics of these de facto reaction shots are similar, sometimes they drew big laughs and sometimes what felt more like hushed suspense. It was as if viewers were deciding moment to moment whether they were watching dark comedy or something more menacing. Though the disparaging of Evans got an enthusiastically cathartic reaction, applause when the movie threw to its end credits was scattered and uncertain.

It’s not unprecedented for a movie to garner audibly mixed reactions. But something Oppenheim and Fielder seem to have cracked is allowing an audience to feel satisfied and impressed by those reactions, which would often serve as a death knell to a prospective blockbuster. When I asked people after the show for their immediate impressions of the film, one woman said it was “funnier than I expected”, while another was surprised by the sympathy she felt for Holmes at times despite feeling “on guard” about what to believe from her.

The most common reaction, however, was a kind of admiring confusion. They weren’t exactly sure what to think, a feeling that’s not traditionally music to a film executive’s ears. Because its initial release was in fewer than a thousand theaters, You Can See Everything hasn’t been subjected to the traditional and finicky CinemaScore polling that asks opening-night audiences for a grade, and seems to inexplicably augur disappointment with anything that’s not at least a B+. But PostTrak, another polling service, shows highly positive results. This could carry the movie past the $100m mark in North America, something only ever accomplished by one other documentary: Michael Moore’s hot-button Fahrenheit 9/11, which had the advantage of election-year currency and a film-maker coming off an Oscar win.

Is this phenom, in conjunction with the surprise smash of Obsession and the less shocking but still staggering success of The Odyssey, indicative of movie audiences willing to grapple with more than they’ve been given credit for in the past? Or, along with the film’s three-hour runtime, is it more of an example of how traditionally TV-based projects are afforded a leeway that narrative films rarely receive from general audiences? As with the movie itself, clear answers haven’t emerged, and probably won’t. At very least, though, it offers some clear respite from the applause-mongering of the IP-driven, fan-focused era. Those movies won’t be banished by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, but by the time the next Avengers rolls around, they might feel, however slightly, like a narrower slice of the cinematic experience.

这是有效地作为一个三个小时的交叉之间的The Dropout和The Rehearsal?", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有一种感觉,这个意想不到的团队是销售的一部分,这个想法的WTF性质是无限的。 然而,额外的承诺似乎是,你可以看到一切会提供一些更令人惊讶和不容易的流动事件。 坐在我旁边的23岁的她说,她从社交媒体 - 具体,Instagram和TikTok的剪辑 - 得到印象,这是“文化时刻”,因为她把它。通过社交媒体的剪辑和听觉泡沫表明,这部电影只是“与其他任何东西不同(在电影中)”并且必须被第一手看到,以便相信 - 或者至少以适当的数量的 spoiler-free,观众-vibing 惊喜体验。 令人惊讶的是,虽然电影已经在一周以上的外面,并已经谈到至少半途到死亡在线,这些二十个观众没有任何关于电影在其半途标志上制作的意想不到的旋转 - 特别令人印象深刻的数据它包含另一个品牌名称添加到混合物。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在電影本身,那個神秘的客人感覺到她在現時獲得球迷;她甚至獲得了一圈自發的鼓勵,描述了霍爾姆斯的伴侶,比利·埃文斯,作為“Batshit瘋狂”。但雖然早期電影被描述為遇到被電影的驚喜引導的誘拐性觀眾的參與,這個人感到更不可預測在其轉變的浪潮的笑聲和模糊的不舒服。她的孩子们,她准备在几周内离开她的监狱判决,两次我观看了它,全观众,菲尔德的反应“这必须是艰难的”吸引了电影的最大笑声之一,似乎是多么平坦的强制性它听起来。电影经常切断到菲尔德在紧张的时刻在福尔摩斯家族的附近沉默;虽然这些事实反应射击的机械类似,有时他们吸引了大笑声,有时感觉更像一个混乱的悬挂。 它似乎观众决定一瞬间,他们是否正在观看黑暗喜剧或更有威胁的东西。", "links": [{"text": "Billy Evans", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/22/you-can-see-everything-elizabeth-holmes-billy-evans-villain"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/57cfb760672c75dd35f22a3e017a21c76ea71e7a/1140_621_1860_1488/master/1860.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Nathan Fielder和Elizabeth Holmes《你可以看到一切》", "caption": "Nathan Fielder和Elizabeth Holmes在You Can See Everything的照片:Everett Collection Inc/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但是,Oppenheim和Fielder似乎已经破裂了一些东西,让观众感到满意和感动这些反应,这往往会作为一个可预见的阻塞器的死亡<unk>子。当我问观众之后他们的电影即时印象时,一个女人说这是“比我预期的更有趣”,而另一个被她对霍尔姆斯的同情感感到惊讶,尽管有时感觉到“在警卫”关于什么值得相信。她。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然而,最常见的反应是一种令人惊叹的混乱. 他们不确定要想什么,感觉这不是传统的音乐在电影执行官的耳朵. 因为它的初始发行是在不到一千个剧院, 你可以看到一切都没有受到传统和最终的CinemaScore调查,要求开放夜间观众一个学位,似乎毫无解释地引起失望的任何东西,至少不是一个B+. 但PostTrak,另一个调查服务,显示了非常积极的结果. 这可能会让电影过去 $100m 北美的标志,仅仅是另一个纪录片所实现的东西:迈克尔·穆尔的热点Fahrenheit 9/11 这是选举年度货币和电影制片人获得奥斯卡奖的优势。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个现象,与被困的惊喜和不那么令人震惊但仍然令人震惊的成功的奥迪赛,指示电影观众愿意玩得比他们在过去的信用更多吗? 或者,与电影的三小时运行时间,它是更多的例子,传统上以电视为基础的项目是如何获得一个短暂的,讲故事电影很少从一般观众获得? 像电影本身一样,明确的答案没有出现,也许是。至少,然而,它提供了一些清晰的敬意,从IP驱动的,粉丝焦点的时代的赞扬,这些电影不会被Nathan Fielder和Lance Oppenheim禁止,但随着下一个冒险者旋转,他们可能会感觉,尽管轻微,像一个更紧的线条的电影体验。", "links": [{"text": "Nathan Fielder", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/nathan-fielder"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "你可以看到一切", "links": [{"text": "You Can See Everything", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/you-can-see-everything"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "纪录片电影", "links": [{"text": "Documentary films", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/documentary"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "纳森·菲尔德", "links": [{"text": "Nathan Fielder", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/nathan-fielder"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "伊丽莎白·福尔摩斯", "links": [{"text": "Elizabeth Holmes", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/elizabeth-holmes"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "特色", "links": [{"text": "features", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/tone/features"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
France ‘s Les Arcs Coproduction Village has unveiled the 17 European feature film projects selected for its 18th edition in December.

One of the most convivial coproduction markets of the year, the showcase is part of the alpine Les Arcs Film Festival ’s Industry Village program, which has previously showcased films such as Oscar-winning animation Flow and Venice Grand Jury Prize winner Vermiglio at the project stage.

This year’s lineup includes France-based Irish British filmmaker Róisín Burns’ debut feature Happy Hardcore about a young Liverpudlian who deserts his post during the Iraq War. The buzzy project previously scooped the Cannes Critics’ Week Next Step prize earlier this year.

Austrian director Bernhard Wenger, whose last film Peacock was his country’s entry for the 2026 Oscars, will present Last Days of Summer. He previously participated in the Les Arcs Talent Village in 2017 with Peacock .

Other returnees include Alexandra Makarová, who presented Perla in the Les Arcs Work in Progress, and comes back with Fanny Is Alive .

Further participants include Finnish director and screenwriter Mikko Myllylahti with Mystery of The Autumn Killer, his second directorial credit after The Woodcutter’s Wife , and Danish Woman at War director Benedikt Erlingsson with Women’s Day .

Three Spanish projects have been selected as part of Les Arcs Film Festival’s wider 2026 country focus devoted to Spain. (scroll down for details in full list below)

A delegation of Spanish professionals, in partnership with the ICAA (Instituto de la Cinematografía y de las Artes Audiovisuales), will attend the Coproduction Village. Additionally, the wider Industry village will host the Spain-France Co-Production Meetings on December 15, organised by ICAA and France’s National Cinema Centre (CNC), bringing together eight Spanish projects in development selected by ICAA with French participants.

The coproduction market, which is part of the alpine Les Arcs Film Festival’s Industry Village program has previously showcased films such as Oscar-winning animation Flow and Venice Grand Jury Prize winner Vermiglio .

It received a record 496 submissions for this year’s edition this year, with the final selection spanning eight first fiction features, five second features and four projects by more established filmmakers.

The projects will compete for the Eurimages Co-production Development Award, worth €20,000 and the ArteKino International Award, worth €6,000.

In addition to the Coproduction showcase, the Industry Village also features a Work In Progress selection; the Talent Village, devoted to eight directors in early development on their first features, and a program of conferences, workshops and masterclasses devoted to hot topics impacting the indie film industry. Details of these strands will be released in the coming weeks.

The Industry Village will take place from December 12 to 15, 2026, as part of the 18th edition of Les Arcs Film Festival, running from December 12 to 19, 2026.
